title: Merging adjacent piles at the cost of the smaller part (min sum of min(L, R)): cubic interval DP vs the closed form S - max s
problem_statement: Given n >= 0 and n + 1 non-negative numbers s_0, ..., s_n (pile sizes in a row; integers or rationals in the implementations), merge the row into a single pile by n merges, each of which joins two adjacent piles of sizes L (left) and R (right) into one pile of size L + R at the cost min(L, R). Compute the smallest possible total cost over all merge orders. Equivalently: the minimum, over all full binary trees whose leaves are s_0, ..., s_n in this order, of the sum over the internal nodes of min(L, R), where L and R are the total sizes of the node's left and right subtree. n = 0 gives 0. With S(x, y) = s_x + ... + s_y this is c(0, n) for c(i, i) = 0, c(i, j) = min_{i<k<=j} [min(S(i, k-1), S(k, j)) + c(i, k-1) + c(k, j)].

input.parameter: n = number of merges (the row has n + 1 piles).
input.size_measure: n + 1 non-negative numbers. Complexities count comparisons of two size-derived values (the comparison model of the entry); additions and subtractions are counted separately in the caveats.

algorithms.name: cubic interval DP (every split)
algorithms.idea: Fill c(i, j) for the rows of piles i..j in order of increasing length; every row tries every split k, i.e. every choice of the blocks i..k-1 and k..j joined by its last merge.
algorithms.pseudocode: prefix sums P; c[i][i] = 0; for L = 1..n, for i = 0..n-L: j = i + L; c[i][j] = min over i < k <= j of (min(P[k] - P[i], P[j+1] - P[k]) + c[i][k-1] + c[k][j]); return c[0][n]
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) on every input: n(n+1)(n+2)/6 candidate splits; exactly n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 comparisons, namely n(n+1)(n+2)/6 inside the merge costs min(L, R) plus (n+1)n(n-1)/6 between candidate values (PROOFS.md, sections 1 and 5)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n^2): the (n + 1) x (n + 1) table c and n + 2 prefix sums (PROOFS.md, section 5)
algorithms.correctness: The merge trees of the row i..j whose last merge joins i..k-1 and k..j are exactly the pairs (merge tree of i..k-1, merge tree of k..j), and such a tree costs min(S(i, k-1), S(k, j)) plus the costs of the two subtrees; induction on j - i. Correct for any sizes. Count, read off the code: a row of length L tries L splits, with one comparison inside each merge cost and L - 1 comparisons between candidates; sum_{L=1..n} (n - L + 1)(2L - 1) = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, of which (n+1)n(n-1)/6 are between candidates. Proof: PROOFS.md, sections 1 and 3.

algorithms.name: closed form S - max s
algorithms.idea: For non-negative sizes the minimum total cost is the total size minus the largest pile: start a caterpillar at a largest pile and add the neighbouring piles one at a time; each added pile is no larger than the block it joins, so it pays its own size, and no merge tree can do better (Proposition, README).
algorithms.pseudocode: total = s_0; largest = s_0; for t = 1..n: total = total + s_t; if s_t > largest: largest = s_t; return total - largest
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n) on every input: exactly n comparisons (the running maximum), n additions and one subtraction, and one pass over the slice sizes[1:] (PROOFS.md, sections 2 and 5)
algorithms.space_complexity: O(n) besides the input: the loop runs over the slice sizes[1:], which CPython builds as a new tuple of n references; otherwise O(1) words (total, largest, the loop variable) (PROOFS.md, section 5)
algorithms.correctness: Proposition (README, with proof): for s_0, ..., s_n >= 0 and every row i..j, c(i, j) = S(i, j) - max(s_i, ..., s_j). Lower bound by induction over the last merge: if it joins blocks of sizes L, R whose largest piles are m_L >= m_R (else mirror), then m_R <= R (a largest pile of a block of non-negative sizes is at most the block's sum) and m_R <= m_L <= L, so m_R <= min(L, R), and the cost is at least min(L, R) + (L - m_L) + (R - m_R) >= L + R - m_L. Upper bound: in the caterpillar from a largest pile, every added pile s joins a block of size at least max s >= s and costs min(block, s) = s, so the total is S - max s. Without the precondition the formula can fail: sizes (-1, 0, 0) give the optimum -2 and the formula -1. Proof: README, section 'The closed form'; the code computes S(0, n) - max s by a loop invariant (PROOFS.md, section 4).

relationship: The cubic interval DP tries all splits of every row, Theta(n^3); for non-negative sizes the closed form S - max s (Proposition, README) answers in Theta(n). Exact comparison counts on every input: n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 vs n (each merge cost min(L, R) counted as one comparison; counting only the comparisons between candidate values, the DP makes (n+1)n(n-1)/6). The closed form also gives an endpoint law (every row has a minimising split at one of its ends), so the endpoint DP is exact here too; the rotation conditions of the split-dependent endpoint law (theorems/endpoint-law-split-dependent-weights) fail for this merge cost on some non-negative sizes, so that note does not give the law for all non-negative sizes (README, with the computations). Proofs: PROOFS.md and the README.

sources.title: Maximum weight triangulation of a special convex polygon
sources.venue: 20th European Workshop on Computational Geometry (EWCG 2004), Seville
sources.note: Credit: Lemma 1 (in a semi-circled convex polygon, one of the two extreme edges belongs to a maximum weight triangulation), an endpoint law for Euclidean chord weights; the entry max-cost-bst-recursion-vs-cubic-dp-vs-endpoint-dp writes its exchange argument out for inclusion-monotone interval weights (Theorem E'). This entry's merge cost depends on the split. The content of Lemma 1 is background.

provenance.note: Elementary. No statement of the closed form was found in the literature checked (README, section 'Literature checked'). This is a statement about that search, not a claim of priority.

verification.method: V1: the validator runs n = 0..10, 12, 16, 25, 40, 70 with 12 instances per n from 12 families of non-negative sizes (bits, small values with many ties, all zero, constant, wide values up to 10^6, one heavy pile, geometric, ramps, sparse, valley, peak, exact rationals). check() is an oracle written separately from the implementations: for n <= 9 it enumerates every merge tree (Catalan(n) trees) and costs it from direct sums; for 10 <= n <= 150 it checks an exact certificate (an explicit caterpillar from a largest pile, costed from direct sums, as the upper bound, and the table B(a, b) = S(a, b) - max(s_a..s_b), accepted only if B(a, b) <= min(S(a, k-1), S(k, b)) + B(a, k-1) + B(k, b) for every split, which bounds every merge tree from below by induction). On every V1 instance check() certified both outputs: it returned True (the validator itself rejects an output only when check() returns False, and requires the implementations to agree), and tests/test_entry_merge_smaller.py asserts True on the whole V1 battery (the validator's seeds, 16 sizes x 12 trials). tests/test_entry_merge_smaller.py: exhaustive equality of the cubic DP, the closed form and the tree enumeration on every size vector with n <= 4 and sizes 0..4, n = 5 and sizes 0..3, and n = 6 and sizes 0..2 (10 188 vectors), with the closed form and an endpoint minimiser in every row of every vector; the exact comparison and arithmetic counts (cubic n = 0..40; closed form n = 0..199, 1000, 4096), each for all 11 integer families; the candidate-only counts (one seeded family per n, n = 0..30); the failures of the mirrored rotation conditions; the table sizes and the size of the numbers (PROOFS.md sections 5 and 6); the endpoint DP on the exhaustive set; the counterexamples of the caveats. V2 (measure 'reported'): the exact number of comparisons of two size-derived values made by the unchanged implementations, counted by the harness's CountingInt number type; generate_scaling draws one of the 11 integer families, and the counts depend on n only. Cost expressions are the exact closed forms: cubic DP n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 (n = 16..128), closed form n (n = 16..4096); rivals cubic n^2, n^2 log n, n^3/log n, n^3 log n, n^4; closed form sqrt(n), log n, n log n, n^2. No counted comparison happens inside a CPython built-in. PROOFS.md proves every claim of the entry (exact counts, correctness, time and space, the size of the numbers, the oracle, the caveats) and names the checks and ranges of each proof.
proofs: PROOFS.md: every claim of the entry (exact counts: sections 1-2; correctness of the cubic DP: 3; the closed form, its code and the endpoint law: 4; time and space: 5; size of the numbers: 6; the V1 oracle: 7; caveats and controls: 8), with the checks and ranges of each proof.
Closed form c(i, j) = S(i, j) - max(s_i..s_j) for sizes >= 0, and the endpoint law derived from it: README, sections 'The closed form' and 'The endpoint law' (written proofs; not machine-checked).

caveats: The closed form needs non-negative sizes; the cubic DP is correct for any sizes. With a negative size the formula can fail: sizes (-1, 0, 0) (n = 2) have the optimum -2 and the formula gives -1. The direction matters: maximising the same total (max sum of min(L, R)) is a different problem, where neither the closed form nor the endpoint rule applies (sizes (1, 1, 1, 1): maximum 4, best caterpillar 3). What is counted: every comparison of two size-derived values, including the one inside each merge cost min(L, R) (the comparison model); the closed form makes n comparisons. Additions and subtractions (exact, checked by the tests): (n + 1) + 2n(n+1)(n+2)/3 for the cubic DP (n + 1 for the prefix sums, 4 for each of the n(n+1)(n+2)/6 candidate splits) and n + 1 for the closed form (n additions, one subtraction); index arithmetic is not counted. No lower bound is claimed. Exact arithmetic is assumed; for sizes >= 0 every number the cubic DP computes lies between 0 and n times the total size (PROOFS.md, section 6).
notes: The cubic DP is correct for every merge cost; the closed form uses the specific cost min(L, R). The endpoint law holds here (every row has a minimising split at one of its ends), but it is derived from the closed form: the min forms of Theorem 1 and Corollary 2 of theorems/endpoint-law-split-dependent-weights need the conditions RS3 and RS3w for -w, and both fail for this merge cost on some non-negative sizes (README, with the computations). Relatives: max-merge-cost-larger-part-cubic-dp-vs-endpoint-dp (merge cost max(L, R), maximised) and max-merge-imbalance-cubic-dp-vs-endpoint-dp (merge cost |L - R|, maximised).

background.statement: In a semi-circled convex polygon, one of the two extreme edges belongs to a maximum weight triangulation; the exchange argument of the proof uses only that nested chords are shorter.
